title: Postoperative hyponatraemia: new confusion on day 2

header.contentArea: Perioperative care: fluid and electrolyte disorders (results released in stages)
guidelineVersions: Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance on symptomatic hyponatraemia (Endocr Connect 2016; revised 2022)
ESE/ESICM/ERBP clinical practice guideline on hyponatraemia (Eur J Endocrinol, March 2014)

related.why: Delirium in the older surgical patient: the other causes of new confusion
Postoperative fluid balance and acute kidney injury
Sepsis after emergency laparotomy, a coexisting cause of confusion to exclude

brief.scenario: Mr Andrew Pilbeam, 72, is on day 2 after an emergency laparotomy and small bowel resection for adhesional obstruction. The nurse reports he has become confused this evening. His sodium this afternoon was 125 mmol/L; before surgery it was 139 mmol/L.
brief.task: The examiner will give you his observations, fluid chart and results in stages. Interpret them and discuss your management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Sodium 125 with new confusion is symptomatic and acute. Symptoms, not the number, set the urgency.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Fluid restriction alone for a confused patient, or a litre of 0.9% saline without a diagnosis.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd see him now: ABCDE, GCS, glucose, and look for other causes of confusion."

flow: Read the fluid chart and results

grid.label: Assess the confused patient
grid.fail: Treats the result over the phone without seeing him or considering other causes of confusion.
grid.pass: Sees him: ABCDE, GCS, glucose, observations and fluid balance; considers sepsis, hypoxia, opioids and anastomotic leak as well.
grid.high: Asks specifically about vomiting, seizures and drowsiness, which change urgency; repeats the sodium on a blood gas now.

grid.label: Grade severity and timing
grid.fail: Calls this mild, or misses that the sodium has fallen within two days.
grid.pass: Moderate hyponatraemia (125 to 129 mmol/L) with moderately severe symptoms (confusion); a documented fall within 48 hours makes it acute.
grid.high: Explains that symptoms, not the number, drive treatment, and that an acute fall risks cerebral oedema.

grid.label: Find the cause from the chart and results
grid.fail: Labels it SIADH without assessing volume status, or does not look at the fluid chart.
grid.pass: Low serum osmolality, concentrated urine with a high urine sodium, clinically euvolaemic: an SIADH picture made worse by hypotonic dextrose-saline.
grid.high: Links the SIADH to pain, nausea, opioids and surgery; checks cortisol and thyroid function because SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion.

grid.label: Treat symptomatic hyponatraemia (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Fluid restriction alone, or 0.9% saline, for a confused patient.
grid.pass: Senior and critical care input; 150 ml of 3% saline IV over 20 minutes, recheck sodium, repeat up to twice until it rises by 5.
grid.high: Gives it where he can be monitored closely; stops boluses once symptoms improve; knows 0.9% saline can worsen SIADH.

grid.label: Limit the rate of correction
grid.fail: Aims to normalise the sodium today, or sets no upper limit.
grid.pass: Limits the rise to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L per 24 hours after; checks sodium at 6 and 12 hours.
grid.high: Names osmotic demyelination; if overcorrecting, stops hypertonic fluid and seeks specialist advice on hypotonic fluid with or without desmopressin.

grid.label: Stop the cause, escalate and explain
grid.fail: Leaves the dextrose-saline running and does not tell a senior.
grid.pass: Stops hypotonic fluid, reviews opioids and antiemetics, informs the registrar, documents, explains to him and his family.
grid.high: Involves endocrinology early; once symptoms settle, plans fluid restriction and tailors any IV maintenance to his losses.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The nurse rings: sodium 125 and he's confused. What do you do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd prescribe fluid restriction to a litre a day and recheck the sodium in the morning.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's only 125, so it's mild. He's probably just confused from the anaesthetic.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: His sodium was 139 two days ago. Anything else?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd give a bag of normal saline to bring it up and aim to get it back to normal by tomorrow.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What fluid has he been on?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd carry on with his current fluids; he still needs maintenance.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The nurse rings: sodium 125 and he's confused. What do you do?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd see him now: ABCDE, GCS, glucose, observations and fluid balance. I'd also look for sepsis, hypoxia, opioid toxicity and an anastomotic leak.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Moderate hyponatraemia, 125 to 129, with moderately severe symptoms because he's confused. It fell from 139 within 48 hours, so it's acute.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: He looks euvolaemic. Serum osmolality 262, urine osmolality 460, urine sodium 52. He's had three litres of dextrose-saline.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hypotonic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and a high urine sodium in a euvolaemic patient: an SIADH picture, worsened by hypotonic fluid.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: He's symptomatic, so I'd call my registrar and critical care. 150 ml of 3% saline over 20 minutes, recheck the sodium, and repeat up to twice until it's risen by 5.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No more than 10 in the first 24 hours and 8 a day after that, with sodium checks at 6 and 12 hours.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Stop the dextrose-saline, review his opioids and antiemetics, document, and explain to him and his family what's happening.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The nurse rings: sodium 125 and he's confused.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll see him now. Has he vomited, had a fit or become drowsy? Those make it more urgent. I'll repeat the sodium on a gas while I assess him.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The symptoms matter more than the number. A fall this fast gives the brain no time to adapt, so the risk is cerebral oedema.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The picture fits: pain, nausea, morphine and surgery all drive ADH. But it's a diagnosis of exclusion, so I'd send cortisol and thyroid function before labelling it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In SIADH the kidney keeps the water and excretes the sodium, so 0.9% saline can lower it further. He needs 3% saline in a monitored setting, and I'd stop the boluses once his confusion improves.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Six hours later his sodium is 133.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's 8 already, so he's close to the 24-hour limit of 10. I'd stop all hypertonic fluid. If it overshoots, I'd ask the endocrinologist about hypotonic fluid with or without desmopressin to avoid osmotic demyelination.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Endocrinology advice today. Once he's settled, fluid restriction, with any IV maintenance matched to his NG losses rather than a routine dextrose-saline bag.

failures.move: Fluid restriction alone, or 0.9% saline, for a confused patient with acute hyponatraemia.
failures.consequence: Cerebral oedema can progress to seizures and coma; saline may lower the sodium further in SIADH.

failures.move: Aiming to normalise the sodium within a day.
failures.consequence: Overcorrection risks osmotic demyelination, which can cause permanent neurological disability.

failures.move: Calling it SIADH without assessing volume status or excluding adrenal and thyroid causes.
failures.consequence: Hypovolaemia or adrenal insufficiency is treated wrongly and he deteriorates.
The cause continues and the sodium keeps falling.

recovery.line: Because he's confused, I'd treat this as symptomatic first: hypertonic saline with senior input, then fluid restriction once he's settled.
I'd target symptom relief and a rise of about 5, not a normal number, keeping within 10 in the first 24 hours.

knowledge.fact: Moderate hyponatraemia is 125 to 129 mmol/L, profound below 125; acute means documented within 48 hours.
Confusion, headache and nausea without vomiting are moderately severe symptoms; vomiting, seizures and reduced consciousness are severe.
Both groups need 150 ml of 3% saline IV over 20 minutes, repeated up to twice until the sodium rises by 5 mmol/L.
Limit the rise to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L per 24 hours thereafter.
Postoperative pain, nausea and opioids stimulate ADH; hypotonic maintenance fluid then lowers the sodium.

recall.say: "Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia: he needs hypertonic saline with senior input."

numbers.meaning: repeat up to twice, target rise 5
maximum rise in first 24 h, then each 24 h

recall.trap: Fluid restriction or 0.9% saline for a confused patient.
recall.finish: Hypertonic saline, then fluid restriction for SIADH.

sources.name: Society for Endocrinology Endocrine Emergency Guidance: Emergency management of severe and moderately severely symptomatic hyponatraemia in adult patients (Ball S, Barth J, Levy M; update of Endocr Connect 2016;5:G4-G6)
sources.supports: Severe symptoms (persistent vomiting, seizures, reduced consciousness, cardiorespiratory arrest) and moderately severe symptoms (confusion, headache, nausea without vomiting) both need immediate IV hypertonic saline: 150 ml 3% over 20 minutes, repeated up to twice until a 5 mmol/L rise; limit the rise to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L per 24 hours thereafter; check sodium at 6 and 12 hours and daily; if limits are exceeded, stop hypertonic fluid and consider hypotonic fluid with or without desmopressin

sources.name: Spasovski G, Vanholder R, Allolio B, et al. Clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia (ESE, ESICM, ERBP). Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1-G47
sources.supports: Biochemical severity: mild 130-135, moderate 125-129, profound below 125 mmol/L; acute hyponatraemia documented to have developed within 48 hours; classification by symptoms; correction limits of 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours and 8 mmol/L in each subsequent 24 hours; diagnostic approach using serum osmolality, urine osmolality and urine sodium

partner.opening: Mr Pilbeam is on day 2 after an emergency laparotomy. The nurse has called you because he is confused and his sodium is 125 mmol/L. What would you do?

reveals.trigger: Asks for observations or assesses him (stage 1)
reveals.finding: T 37.6°C, HR 92, BP 138/80, RR 18, SpO2 96% on air. GCS 14 (confused). Capillary glucose 6.8 mmol/L. Nauseated, no vomiting, no seizures. Abdomen soft, wound clean. Moist mucosa, JVP not raised, no oedema.

reveals.trigger: Asks for the fluid and drug charts (stage 2)
reveals.finding: Last 24 hours: 3,000 ml 0.18% sodium chloride in 4% glucose IV; NG aspirate 300 ml; urine 1,100 ml. Morphine PCA and ondansetron. No diuretics.
Na 125 mmol/L (139 pre-op, 131 day 1), K 3.9, urea 4.1, creatinine 78, glucose 6.8. Serum osmolality 262 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality 460 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L. Cortisol and TSH sent.

push.question: How would you assess him?
push.expect: See him now: ABCDE, GCS, glucose, fluid balance; exclude sepsis, hypoxia, opioids, leak.

push.question: How severe is this?
push.expect: Moderate biochemically, moderately severe symptoms, acute (within 48 hours).

push.question: What do the fluid chart and results show?
push.expect: Hypotonic hyponatraemia, euvolaemic, concentrated urine, high urine sodium: SIADH picture plus hypotonic fluid.

push.question: How will you treat him?
push.expect: Senior and critical care input; 150 ml 3% saline over 20 minutes; recheck; up to three boluses.

push.question: How fast can the sodium rise?
push.expect: No more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours, then 8 per 24 hours; check at 6 and 12 hours.

push.question: What else will you do?
push.expect: Stop dextrose-saline; review opioids and antiemetics; registrar; document; explain to patient and family.

curveballs.prompt: He has a generalised seizure while you are talking.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Severe symptoms: ABC, treat the seizure, call for senior and critical care help, give 150 ml 3% saline now and repeat as needed.

curveballs.prompt: Six hours after one bolus he is lucid and his sodium is 131.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Stop hypertonic saline; only 4 mmol/L more is allowed in the first 24 hours; recheck at 12 hours; then fluid restriction.
Escalate now: critical care or pharmacy can supply it; do not substitute a litre of 0.9% saline.

curveballs.prompt: His wife asks if he has had a stroke.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain that a low salt level in the blood is the likely cause, it is being treated, and he is being monitored closely.
